outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Statutory Architecture Behind the Dispute
outline.description: This chapter introduces the statutory scheme that made the case possible. It explains the Office of Special Counsel’s role under the Civil Service Reform Act, the difference between corrective and disciplinary proceedings, and the two separate statutory pathways tied to alleged arbitrary FOIA withholdings. Understanding these provisions is essential because the entire lawsuit turned on whether AFL could force OSC to investigate under one provision despite the limits of another.
subtopics: The Office of Special Counsel as an investigative and prosecutorial agency in the federal civil-service system
OSC’s authority over prohibited personnel practices under 5 U.S.C. § 1214
Disciplinary proceedings under 5 U.S.C. § 1215 and the role of the Merit Systems Protection Board
Section 1214’s procedural features, including notice obligations to the complaining party
Section 1216 as a separate grant of authority to investigate certain misconduct, including arbitrary or capricious FOIA withholding
The text of 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3): OSC 'shall' investigate allegations concerning prohibited FOIA withholdings
Section 1216(c) and its statement that OSC may seek corrective or disciplinary action 'in the same way' as if a prohibited personnel practice were involved
FOIA’s own OSC-related enforcement provision, 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F)(i), and its three statutory predicates
The latent statutory tension: whether FOIA’s specific referral provision limits or coexists with OSC’s broader authority under § 1216

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Facts, Claims, and the Case’s Procedural Path
outline.description: This chapter traces how the controversy arose and how it moved through the district court. It shows the relationship between AFL’s underlying FOIA dispute with DOJ and its separate effort to compel OSC to investigate DOJ’s alleged policy. It also explains the district court’s unusual disposition: partially agreeing with AFL’s statutory reading while still refusing to compel an investigation.
subtopics: AFL’s effort to investigate judicial recusals through a FOIA request to the Department of Justice
The requested records: emails between an outside attorney and DOJ’s Civil Division
AFL’s allegation that DOJ relied on an unlawful policy of not searching employee emails without employee consent
The separate FOIA suit against DOJ and DOJ’s ongoing production of responsive records
Why the adequacy of DOJ’s production was not the issue in this appeal
AFL’s request that OSC investigate DOJ under § 1216(a)(3)
OSC’s response that it lacked authority because FOIA’s § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) predicates had not been satisfied
AFL’s suit against OSC to compel an investigation notwithstanding the FOIA-specific provision
The district court’s ruling that § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) does not limit OSC’s investigative power under § 1216
The district court’s further ruling that whether to investigate or pursue action remained committed to OSC’s discretion under § 1216(c)
The remand to OSC, OSC’s renewed refusal to investigate, the entry of final judgment, and AFL’s appeal
The court of appeals’ de novo review and its decision to raise standing on its own before reaching the merits

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Article III Standing as a Threshold Barrier
outline.description: This chapter explains why the D.C. Circuit never resolved the merits. It sets out the constitutional requirement of standing, the court’s duty to address jurisdiction first, and the special rules governing alleged procedural injuries. The chapter highlights the key doctrinal move in the opinion: AFL tried to reframe OSC’s noninvestigation as a denial of procedural rights tied to informational harms, but the court held that this still required a concrete injury, causation, and redressability.
subtopics: Why federal courts must decide jurisdiction before merits under Article III
The core standing elements from Lujan: injury in fact, causation, and redressability
The requirement that injury be concrete, particularized, and actual or imminent
Pleading standing at the motion-to-dismiss stage
AFL’s supplemental briefing after the D.C. Circuit requested briefing on standing
AFL’s claimed procedural right to an OSC investigation under § 1216
The rule from Summers that a bare procedural violation, without an affected concrete interest, is not enough
The D.C. Circuit’s framework for procedural-injury cases: relaxed imminence and redressability, but not injury in fact or causation
Why the court did not need to decide whether AFL’s asserted injuries were procedural or substantive
The opinion’s overall structure: testing each of AFL’s two standing theories separately

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: AFL’s First Theory of Standing—Loss of the Requested FOIA Records
outline.description: This chapter examines AFL’s first asserted injury: that OSC’s refusal to investigate prevented AFL from obtaining the DOJ records it sought through FOIA. The court rejected this theory because the alleged injury was caused directly by DOJ, not OSC, and because the chain from an OSC investigation to eventual document production depended on multiple speculative decisions by independent actors.
subtopics: AFL’s argument that the absence of an OSC investigation deprived it of the records sought from DOJ
The court’s identification of the real source of the informational injury: DOJ’s withholding, not OSC’s inaction
Traceability problems when the defendant is not the actor directly denying the information
The court’s step-by-step causal chain: OSC investigation, possible OSC enforcement action, possible MSPB sanctions, possible DOJ change in conduct
Why that chain was too speculative and attenuated to satisfy Article III
The significance of independent actors not before the court: OSC, MSPB, and DOJ
Use of FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine on causation and speculation about third-party choices
Use of Heckler v. Chaney on enforcement discretion and the limits of judicial compulsion
Redressability and the need to show that a favorable judgment would likely spur the events needed to remedy the injury
Use of Hecate Energy and Haaland v. Brackeen to emphasize that redressability turns on binding effects, not persuasive influence
Why AFL’s interest in obtaining DOJ records could not support standing against OSC even under a relaxed procedural-injury framework

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 5: AFL’s Second Theory of Standing, the Court’s Disposition, and the Case’s Significance
outline.description: This final chapter addresses AFL’s alternative claim of informational injury based on the investigation itself. The court held that informational standing requires a statutory entitlement to receive information, and § 1216 provides no such entitlement. Because OSC was not required to import § 1214’s notice provisions into a § 1216 investigation, AFL lacked both a concrete informational injury and redressability. The chapter concludes with the jurisdictional disposition and the opinion’s practical lessons.
subtopics: AFL’s second theory: loss of notices or information that might arise from an OSC investigation
The doctrine of informational standing and the requirement of a statutory entitlement to receive information
The court’s reliance on Akins, Public Citizen, and related D.C. Circuit precedent
Why § 1216(a)(3), even if mandatory as to investigation, does not itself entitle the complainant to information
AFL’s fallback reliance on § 1214’s notice provisions
The key concession that OSC need not apply § 1214’s procedural notice requirements in a § 1216 investigation
The role of Carson v. Office of Special Counsel in treating § 1214 procedures as discretionary in the § 1216 context
Failure of injury in fact: no denial of information to which AFL was legally entitled
Failure of redressability: even a court order requiring an investigation would not likely produce the notices AFL wanted
The appellate disposition: vacatur of the district court’s merits judgment and remand with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
The difference between a merits loss and a jurisdictional dismissal
Significance of the opinion for suits seeking to compel agency investigations, especially where the plaintiff’s asserted injury depends on third-party enforcement decisions
The case’s broader lesson: statutory 'shall' language does not eliminate Article III’s independent demand for concrete, redressable injury
